title: Introduce user-mode aggregation slab and kernel-selection cache to cut host-side memcpy and thread churn
creator: Asha Patel
description: Host-side overhead for mixed prefill/decode workloads is a major contributor to tail latency and CPU cost. Small, frequent buffer copies and repeated kernel-probing on first requests increase syscall and thread scheduling churn. This ticket implements a lightweight user-mode aggregation slab (short-lived buffer aggregator) plus a kernel-selection cache and handshake hint to reduce copies, avoid repeated kernel probes, and smooth threadpool contention during bursty traffic.
background: In production traces we see many small host->GPU memcpy operations interleaved with decode work, and multiple threads attempting kernel probes for the same model/sequence-length vector. Previous efforts reduced copying at the kernel layer but left a gap where host thread scheduling and per-request memcpy spikes persist under short bursts. We also observe repeated runtime kernel selection work on warm requests that could be cached per-model+shape signature.
solution_overview: 1) Implement a user-mode aggregation slab that coalesces small host buffers destined for the same GPU device into a single pinned DMA batch and exposes a single memcpy syscall per cohort. 2) Add a compact kernel-selection cache keyed by (model-id, kv-cache-length-distribution, dtype, quantization-profile) to fast-path kernel choice on hot paths. 3) Introduce a lightweight handshake hint that lets the host thread indicate 'prefill-only' vs 'decode-hot' intent to the threadpool scheduler to avoid needless preemption and wakeups.
design_decisions: Use a lock-free MPSC ring for slab allocation to minimize syscall latency in common path
Keep slab lifetimes < 8ms to avoid interfering with KV cache locality and GPU memory pressure
Kernel-selection cache is bounded (256 entries) and uses an LRU eviction to prefer recent shapes; cache entries include kernel_id and micro-tuning flags
Handshake hint implemented as thread-local flag with short-lived window, avoids cross-thread atomics for the common case
Fallback: if aggregation slab is full or shapes incompatible, fall back to current zero-copy path to preserve correctness
progress_updates: 2025-02-15: Spike prototyped aggregation slab in user-space; microbench shows 35% reduction in memcpy syscalls for synthetic small-batch prefill workload
2025-02-20: Implemented kernel-selection cache prototype and wired to model loader; local microbench shows kernel probe reduced from ~1.8ms to ~0.12ms on hit
2025-02-24: End-to-end integration test added; observed 10% P50 and 18% P95 end-to-end latency improvements on prefill-heavy traces in staging
2025-02-27: Identified threadpool starvation edge-case when many long-lived decode threads hold slab reservations; added short backoff and eviction path to mitigate
2025-03-01: Created initial PR and performance comparison dashboard; preparing canary rollout steps
acceptance_criteria: Canary on runtime-1.20 shows >=10% P50 and >=15% P95 reduction on prefill-heavy customer workload compared to baseline
System CPU user+sys consumption for host process reduced by >=12% in the same canary window
Memcpy syscall rate (host->gpu) reduced by >=30% for small-batch workloads as measured by perf counters
No regression in model output correctness or quantization behavior (smoke eval against golden prompts)
Feature gated behind a runtime flag and rolled back cleanly within 30 minutes if issues observed
risks: Aggregation slab introduces transient memory pressure on pinned buffers; could increase OOM risk in corner cases
Kernel-selection cache might return suboptimal kernel for rare shape combos leading to latency spikes; monitoring required
Handshake hint semantics could interact badly with existing autoscaling heuristics if not throttled
Complexity in debugging host-side coalescing may increase time-to-triage for customer incidents
